screens.title: Dynamic Environments and Review Apps Defined
screens.narratorSegment: At its core, a Dynamic Environment is an on-demand, temporary environment created for a specific purpose, such as testing a feature branch. Think of it as a dedicated sandbox that springs into existence when needed and disappears when its purpose is served. A Review App is a specialized type of dynamic environment, automatically deployed for each new merge request. This means that every time a developer pushes changes to a feature branch and opens a merge request, GitLab CI/CD can automatically build and deploy a live version of that branch. This live deployment provides a unique, isolated environment where anyone—from fellow developers to product managers and testers—can interact with the changes directly in a browser. This eliminates the common bottleneck of shared staging environments, where multiple features might be waiting in a queue, leading to delays and potential conflicts. It's about giving every feature its own dedicated stage for review. Dynamic Environments and Review Apps Defined means dynamic environments and review apps provide isolated, temporary deployments for feature branches, eliminating shared environment bottlenecks.. In practical terms, isolated, temporary deployments for feature branches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Review Apps eliminate shared staging bottlenecks by providing unique, isolated environments for every feature branch, accelerating feedback.

screens.title: The Substantial Benefits of Review Apps
screens.narratorSegment: The advantages of integrating Review Apps into your CI/CD pipeline are truly substantial, impacting every stage of your development cycle. Firstly, they provide accelerated feedback. Developers and designers get immediate visual feedback on their changes, allowing for quick iterations and corrections. Imagine seeing your UI changes live within minutes of pushing code, rather than waiting for a manual deployment. Secondly, Review Apps significantly improve collaboration. Non-technical stakeholders, like product managers or marketing teams, can easily preview features without needing to pull code, set up local environments, or even understand the underlying technical details. This democratizes the review process. Thirdly, they enable early bug detection. Testers can find bugs much earlier in the development cycle, when they are less costly and complex to fix. This shifts quality assurance left, saving valuable time and resources. Fourthly, Review Apps reduce bottlenecks by eliminating the need to queue for a shared staging environment, which often becomes a choke point. Finally, they enhance code review by providing a live demonstration of the changes, complementing static code analysis. This means reviewers can not only read the code but also interact with its functionality, leading to more thorough and effective reviews. These benefits collectively lead to faster delivery of higher-quality software.

screens.title: Configuring Review Apps with CI/CD Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing Review Apps in GitLab CI/CD relies heavily on the environment keyword, which we've touched upon previously. The real power comes from its ability to define dynamic names and URLs using predefined CI/CD variables. These variables allow each Review App to have a unique identity and a distinct web address, preventing conflicts and ensuring isolation. The most commonly used variable for this purpose is $CI underscore COMMIT underscore REF underscore SLUG. This variable provides a 'slugified' version of your branch name, meaning it converts characters that aren't URL-friendly, like slashes or spaces, into hyphens. For example, a branch named feature slash my-new-feature would become feature-my-new-feature. This slug is perfect for creating unique subdomains or path segments for your Review Apps. By using this variable, you ensure that every merge request automatically gets its own dedicated, accessible environment without manual intervention, making the process highly scalable and efficient. This dynamic naming convention is fundamental to the Review App pattern. Configuring Review Apps with CI/CD Variables means the `environment` keyword combined with `$ci_commit_ref_slug` enables unique, dynamic names and urls for each review app.. In practical terms, leveraging dynamic names and urls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Configuring Review Apps
Configuration Basics

Configuring Review Apps with CI/CD Variables

Leveraging Dynamic Names and URLs

The `environment` Keyword

Defines deployment environments, crucial for managing dynamic Review Apps.

`$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` Variable

Provides a URL-friendly version of the branch name (e.g., `feature/new-ui` becomes `feature-new-ui`).

Key Takeaway

Using `$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` with the `environment` keyword is fundamental for creating unique, isolated Review App deployments.

Example: Dynamic Environment Configuration
deploy_review_app:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - echo "Deploying review app..."
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG # Dynamic name
    url: https://$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.review.example.com # Dynamic URL
    on_stop: stop_review_app
  only:
    - branches
  except:
    - main
Variable in Action

Branch: feature/new-dashboard

$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG: feature-new-dashboard

Resulting URL: https://feature-new-dashboard.review.example.com

screens.title: The Build Job for Review Apps
screens.narratorSegment: Before we can deploy a Review App, we first need to build our application. This is handled by a dedicated build job in our. gitlab-ci. yml file. Let's examine a typical build underscore app job. This job is responsible for compiling code, running tests, and preparing any static assets or build artifacts that the deployment job will need. Notice the script section, where we might echo messages for debugging and create a public directory to hold our web content. The artifacts keyword is crucial here; it specifies that the contents of the public directory should be saved and passed to subsequent jobs in the pipeline. This ensures that the built application is available for the deployment step. We also use only. - branches and except. - main to ensure this job runs only for feature branches and not for the main production branch, which would typically have its own deployment strategy. This isolation is key to the Review App workflow, ensuring that only relevant branches trigger these temporary deployments. A common mistake here is forgetting to define artifacts, which would prevent the deployment job from finding the necessary files.

keyIdea.title: Build and Artifacts
keyIdea.text: The `build_app` job prepares the application and uses `artifacts` to pass the build output to the deployment job, running only on feature branches.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Build Job for Review Apps
.gitlab-ci.yml: `build_app` job
stages:
  - build
  - deploy
  - cleanup

build_app:
  stage: build
  script:
    - echo "Building application for branch $CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG..."
    - mkdir public
    - echo "<h1>Review App for $CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG</h1>" > public/index.html
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - public # Output of the build, passed to next stages
  only:
    - branches # Run only on branches
  except:
    - main # Exclude the main branch
CI/CD Job Breakdown

The Build Job for Review Apps

Preparing Your Application for Deployment

Purpose of `build_app`

Compiles source code, runs tests, and prepares static assets or other build outputs.

Importance of `artifacts`

Ensures the built application files are available for subsequent deployment jobs.

Key Takeaway

The build job is the first step, creating the deployable assets and making them accessible via `artifacts` for the Review App deployment.

Common Mistake

Forgetting to define `artifacts` will prevent the deployment job from finding the necessary build output, leading to pipeline failures.

This job is where the magic of Review Apps truly happens. In the script section, you'd include commands to deploy your public artifacts to your chosen cloud hosting service, whether that's Netlify, Vercel, an S3 bucket, or a Kubernetes cluster. The environment keyword is critical here. We define name. review slash $CI underscore COMMIT underscore REF underscore SLUG to create a unique environment name for each branch, ensuring isolation. Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Deploying Review App
.gitlab-ci.yml: `deploy_review_app` job
deploy_review_app:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - echo "Deploying review app to a dynamic environment..."
    - # Commands to deploy 'public' to a cloud hosting service
    - echo "Review app for $CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG deployed to $CI_ENVIRONMENT_URL"
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG # Dynamic environment name
    url: https://$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.review.example.com # Dynamic URL based on branch
    on_stop: stop_review_app # Link to the cleanup job
  only:
    - branches
  except:
    - main
  needs: ["build_app"]
Deployment Logic

Deploying the Review App

Provisioning Your Dynamic Environment

Dynamic Naming & URL

`name` and `url` use `$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` for unique, accessible environments.

`on_stop` Parameter

Crucially links to a cleanup job, ensuring resources can be de-provisioned.

Key Takeaway

The `deploy_review_app` job creates the live environment, dynamically named and URL-addressed, and sets up the crucial link for cleanup.

Pro-Tip

Ensure your deployment commands are idempotent, meaning they can be run multiple times without causing unintended side effects.

screens.title: Cleaning Up Review App Resources
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most critical aspects of managing dynamic environments is ensuring proper cleanup. Without it, you risk resource leaks, leading to unexpected cloud costs and clutter. This is where the stop underscore review underscore app job comes into play, linked by the on underscore stop parameter in our deployment job. This cleanup job's script section contains commands to de-provision the resources that were allocated for the Review App. This could involve deleting cloud instances, removing S3 buckets, or using kubectl delete for Kubernetes deployments. The environment keyword is used again, with name. review slash $CI underscore COMMIT underscore REF underscore SLUG to target the specific dynamic environment, and action. stop to explicitly signal GitLab that this job is for stopping an environment. The when. manual keyword is often used here. While it means the job won't run automatically after every pipeline, GitLab intelligently adds a 'Stop environment' button to the merge request widget. This allows you or other team members to manually trigger the cleanup, or GitLab can even trigger it automatically when the associated merge request is closed or merged, preventing resource waste. This mechanism is vital for cost control and maintaining a tidy cloud infrastructure.

keyIdea.text: The `stop_review_app` job, linked by `on_stop` and using `environment: action: stop`, ensures resources are de-provisioned, preventing leaks.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Cleaning Up Review Apps
.gitlab-ci.yml: `stop_review_app` job
stop_review_app:
  stage: cleanup
  script:
    - echo "Stopping review app for branch $CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG..."
    - # Commands to de-provision resources (e.g., delete cloud instances)
    - echo "Review app for $CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG stopped and resources cleaned up."
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    action: stop # Explicitly marks this job for stopping an environment
  when: manual # Allows GitLab to offer a stop button on MR closure
  only:
    - branches
  except:
    - main
Resource Management

Cleaning Up Review App Resources

Preventing Resource Leaks with `on_stop`

Purpose of `stop_review_app`

De-provisions cloud resources associated with a Review App, preventing cost overruns.

`environment: action: stop`

Informs GitLab that this job is intended to stop a specific environment.

Key Takeaway

Properly configured `on_stop` and `stop_review_app` jobs are essential for managing cloud costs and ensuring efficient resource utilization.

Safety Note

screens.title: Avoiding Common Mistakes with Review Apps
screens.narratorSegment: While Review Apps offer immense benefits, there are common pitfalls that teams often encounter. Being aware of these can save you significant headaches and costs. The first major mistake is resource leaks. Forgetting to implement the on underscore stop job, or having a faulty cleanup script, can lead to cloud resources continuously consuming funds. Always test your cleanup thoroughly. A good practice is to regularly audit your active environments. Secondly, permissions issues are frequent. Your CI/CD user or runner needs appropriate permissions to provision and de-provision resources in your cloud provider. Ensure your cloud A P I keys or service accounts have the necessary scope, but also follow the principle of least privilege. Thirdly, naming conflicts can arise if you're not using a unique variable like $CI underscore COMMIT underscore REF underscore SLUG. Accidentally deploying multiple Review Apps to the same environment name will lead to unexpected behavior. Always rely on dynamic variables for uniqueness. Finally, slow provisioning can negate the benefits. If your Review App takes too long to deploy, it can still create a bottleneck. Optimize your deployment scripts, consider using pre-built images, or leverage faster cloud services. By proactively addressing these common issues, you can ensure your Review Apps are robust, secure, and cost-effective.

Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Common Mistakes
Best Practices

Avoiding Common Mistakes with Review Apps

Ensuring Robust and Cost-Effective Deployments

Resource Leaks

Failing to implement or properly test the `on_stop` job can lead to continuous cloud resource consumption and unexpected costs.

Solution: Test `on_stop` thoroughly; audit environments.

Permissions Issues

The CI/CD user needs appropriate permissions to provision and de-provision resources in your cloud provider, often leading to deployment failures.

Solution: Verify CI/CD user permissions; use least privilege.

Naming Conflicts

Not using `$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` or another unique variable can result in multiple Review Apps attempting to deploy to the same environment name.

Solution: Always use dynamic variables for uniqueness.

Slow Provisioning

If the Review App deployment process is too slow, it can negate the benefits of rapid feedback and create new bottlenecks.

Solution: Optimize deployment scripts; use faster services.
Key Takeaway

Proactive management of permissions, unique naming, efficient provisioning, and robust cleanup are crucial for successful and cost-effective Review App implementation.
